text: Both sentences can be translated as "I am a student" (私 = "I" [jmdict-1311110], 学生 = "student" [jmdict-1206900]), but 私は学生です uses は to mark the topic (what the sentence is about, usually known information) and answers "what about me?" [g-wa-001][jmdict-1311110][jmdict-1206900]. 私が学生です uses が to mark the grammatical subject and present it as new information, answering "who is the student?" [g-wa-001][jmdict-1311110][jmdict-1206900].

Because the particle が is used for the object of 好き (the thing that is liked), that thing is marked with が rather than を [g-ga-001]. Therefore you say 日本語が好きです (日本語 is what is liked), not 日本語を好きです [g-ga-001].

「ゲームばかりしている」は「ゲームをすることばかりで、（度が過ぎる・不満の意を含む）」というニュアンスで「〜ばかり」が過度さや批判を含むことを示します [g-bakari-001].  
「ゲームだけしている」は単に「ゲームだけをしている」という限定を表し、判断や批判は含みません [g-dake-001].  
どちらも「〜ている」の形を取っており、文脈次第で進行や結果状態を表すことがあります（動詞によって読みが変わる）[g-teiru-001].

"食べたばかり" means "just ate" — it marks an action completed a short time ago from the speaker's perspective [g-tabakari-001]. It is distinct from the ばかり that means "nothing but" (e.g., ゲームばかり); the た before ばかり is what tells them apart [g-tabakari-001; g-bakari-001].

Use ても when you mean "even if / even though" as a concession — the following clause holds regardless of the condition, and ても attaches to the て-form (the て and も are separate) [g-temo-001]. Use のに when you want to mark a result contrary to expectation and usually express surprise, regret, or complaint (contrast: のに carries complaint while ても is hypothetical and carries no complaint) [g-noni-001].
結婚しているは「結婚している＝is married」で、ているは動作の進行か変化後の状態かどちらかを示すが、結婚の場合は変化後の状態（既に結婚している）を表すとされています [g-teiru-001]. 例として「私は結婚していて子どもが二人いる。」は「I am married and have two children.」と訳されています [tatoeba-5155].

The example uses 知っている to express "know" (仕事を生半可に知っている人が... = people who only know their work imperfectly) rather than the dictionary form 知る [tatoeba-74275]. Therefore the evidence indicates you should use 知っている, not 知る on its own, to mean "I know" [tatoeba-74275].

No — てしまう can mark either simple completion or regret; context decides which meaning dominates [g-teshimau-001]. For example, it often expresses regret (全部食べてしまった “I ate it all (oops)”) and appears in exclamations of having blundered (し、しまったぁ！) [g-teshimau-001][tatoeba-74516].

They both express ability meaning "can / be able to" [jmdict-1004550][g-kotogadekiru-001]. 話すことができる is the dictionary-form + ことができる potential and is more formal than the potential verb form 話せる [g-kotogadekiru-001].

降るそうだは「聞いた話」で「降る（plain）＋そうだ＝I hear it will rain」の形で使います[g-souda-hearsay-001].  
降りそうだは「様態・見た目」で「降り（verb stem）＋そうだ＝it looks like it will rain」となり、形状詞として動詞の語幹に付く点で区別されます[g-souda-appearance-001].
ようだ expresses the speaker's inference based on evidence (e.g. 雨が降るようだ = "it seems it will rain") [g-youda-001]. It is described as softer and more subjective than らしい [g-youda-001].
NOT_FOUND

No — は marks the topic, not necessarily the grammatical subject [g-wa-001]. が is the particle that marks the grammatical subject and presents it as new or identifying information, so は and が contrast (e.g. 私は学生です vs 私が学生です) [g-ga-001][g-wa-001].
ているは「動作の進行」か「変化後の状態」を表す二つの読み方があり、どちらになるかは動詞によって決まると明示されています [g-teiru-001]. したがって、すべての動詞に付ければ常に進行形になるわけではなく、動詞によっては進行ではなく結果状態を表します [g-teiru-001].
NOT_FOUND

Yes. The particle ばかり expresses "nothing but/only" and “limits by implying excess,” often carrying a critical nuance [g-bakari-001]. With ている showing a progressive/habitual action, 魚ばかり食べている reads as "does nothing but eat fish," which carries that same critical implication [g-bakari-001][g-teiru-001].
食べてしまいなさいは、てしまうを使って「（それを）食べてしまいなさい＝食べて全部終えてしまいなさい／食べ尽くしなさい」という意味を表します [g-teshimau-001]。文脈によっては単なる完了を示すか、後悔のニュアンスを帯びることがあります [g-teshimau-001].
No. ことができる is built from the dictionary (non‑past) form + ことができる, so you should say 食べることができる rather than 食べたことができる [g-kotogadekiru-001; jmdict-1004550].
NOT_FOUND

No. ようだ expresses the speaker's inference from evidence (e.g. 雨が降るようだ) and is described as the speaker's inference, not hearsay [g-youda-001]. By contrast, hearsay is expressed by the hearsay そうだ which attaches to the plain form (降るそうだ), with appearance そうだ treated separately [g-souda-appearance-001].

Because they are two different そう: the appearance そう attaches to the stem (so the adjective becomes 高+そう＝高そうだ) while the hearsay そう attaches to the plain form (高い+そう＝高いそうだ) [g-souda-appearance-001][g-souda-hearsay-001]. The grammar notes even say the tokenizer treats appearance そう as 形状詞 and hearsay そう as 名詞, reflecting that they behave differently [g-souda-appearance-001].

が is used to mark the grammatical subject and to present that subject as new or identifying information [g-ga-001]. It is used instead of は when you want to single out or identify who is the subject (私が学生です answers “who is the student?”) because は marks a known topic [g-wa-001]. が is also used for the object of verbs like 好き、嫌い、上手、できる [g-ga-001].
